turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not pleased, Mr. Worthing, with the vagueness of your replies so far. Please, do not attempt to obscure the truth from me.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, I am being perfectly frank, but I'm afraid I don't know how to explain certain things very well.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, sir, do not be coy with me!

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I beg your pardon, Lady Bracknell, I am not trying to be coy, but I am rather hesitant to speak about my family, as it is not a terribly... respectable one, I'm afraid.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, Mr. Worthing, if your family is not respectable, I daresay that is a trifling matter in comparison to your own personal character. I must confess, I am not impressed by your attempt to gloss over the subject.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't wish to conceal the truth, Lady Bracknell. My family's history is, shall we say, somewhat... complicated.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I do not understand what you mean by 'complicated', Mr. Worthing. Pray, be more explicit.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I'm afraid I'm not very good at explaining things, Lady Bracknell. It's just that my life has been rather... unusual, and I'm not sure how to put it into words.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I daresay, 'unusual' is a charitable description of your circumstances, Mr. Worthing. Now, pray tell, what is it that you do for a living?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Good heavens, Mother, must we interrogate him like a suspect in a courtroom? Can't you see I'm perfectly capable of making my own decisions about my life?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I assure you, Lady Bracknell, I'm not trying to be uncooperative, it's just that I'm a bit... overwhelmed by all these questions.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am not accustomed to being treated with such levity, Mr. Worthing. Your responses thus far have been woefully inadequate.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do hope you're not going to continue this inquisition much longer, Mother. I'm beginning to feel like I'm being interrogated rather than Jack.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I'm afraid I've said as much as I can, Lady Bracknell. I assure you, my intentions towards your daughter are entirely honourable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your reserve is quite puzzling. I had expected a more forthcoming young man, considering the prospect of marrying my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I'm afraid I'm not quite sure what you mean, Lady Bracknell. I've always tried to be straightforward, but I suppose I may not be very good at it.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, sir, I do believe you are trying to be facetious, but I must warn you that it is not becoming in a man who aspires to marry my daughter. Your lack of clarity is quite... distressing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I'm afraid I don't mean to be facetious, Lady Bracknell. I'm simply a humble man trying to do what's right.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Good heavens, young man, do not attempt to be facetious with me. I have no patience for such frivolity.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I didn't mean to be facetious, Lady Bracknell. I'm just a bit...overwhelmed by the conversation.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
